title: Custom Impression Trays & Master Casts — Test

mcqs.q: A custom tray is best defined as:
opts: An individualized impression tray made from a cast recovered from a preliminary impression
A prefabricated tray selected to fit an average arch
A tray used only for the preliminary impression
A metal tray used for elastomeric impressions
mcqs.explain: It is used in making the final impression, whereas the stock tray is used for the preliminary impression.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the stated reasons for using a custom tray?
opts: To shorten the laboratory time of the case
To confine and control the final impression material
Development of the border seal
To ensure planned distribution of pressure on the residual ridges
mcqs.explain: The five reasons are: confine and control the material, obtain minute details of the denture-bearing area, develop the border seal, ensure uniform distribution of material, and ensure planned distribution of pressure.

mcqs.q: The two materials used for custom trays are:
opts: Chemically-cured acrylic resin and visible light-cured resin
Impression compound and shellac
Dental stone and impression plaster
Polyether and polysulfide
mcqs.explain: Polyether and polysulfide are final impression materials, not tray materials.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the chemically-cured acrylic resin tray material?
opts: Rigid, easy to fabricate, easy to trim and adjust, and inexpensive
Free of any polymerization shrinkage
Can be used immediately after fabrication
Contains no monomer
mcqs.explain: Its disadvantages are polymerization shrinkage, the waiting interval before use, and the hazards of the monomer.

mcqs.q: A time interval must be allowed between fabrication and use of a chemically-cured custom tray because of:
opts: Polymerization shrinkage
Water sorption
Thermal expansion
Monomer evaporation making it brittle
mcqs.explain: Using the tray too early means taking the impression in a tray whose shape is still changing.

mcqs.q: The hazardous effects of the monomer used in chemically-cured tray resin include:
opts: Dermatologic reactions
Permanent staining of the teeth
Loss of taste sensation
Corrosion of metal instruments
mcqs.explain: The monomer is methyl methacrylate.

mcqs.q: The chemical name of visible light-cured tray resin is:
opts: Urethane dimethacrylate
Methyl methacrylate
Polyvinyl siloxane
Zinc oxide eugenol
mcqs.explain: It is available in sheet and gel forms; the sheet form is used for tray fabrication.

mcqs.q: VLC tray material is used for tray fabrication in which form?
opts: Sheet form
Gel form
Powder form
Cartridge form
mcqs.explain: It is available in both sheet and gel forms, but sheets are used for trays.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of visible light-cured tray resin?
opts: It is brittle and needs a special curing chamber
It is very hazardous to handle
It greatly increases preparation time
It has poor handling properties
mcqs.explain: Its advantages are that it is less hazardous, reduces preparation time, is easy to use and has good handling properties; it also produces fine particles during grinding.

mcqs.q: The first pencil line drawn on the cast marks the:
opts: Anticipated final extension of the denture
Spacer outline
Tray outline
Position of the tissue stops
mcqs.explain: The tray outline and then the spacer outline are drawn progressively inside it.

mcqs.q: The tray extension is marked in pencil about:
opts: 2 mm shorter than the first pencil line, except in the posterior palatal seal area
2 mm longer than the first pencil line
5 mm shorter than the first pencil line
Exactly on the first pencil line
mcqs.explain: The border molding material, not the rigid tray, is intended to reach the full sulcus depth.

mcqs.q: The spacer outline is marked:
opts: 2 mm short of the tray outline
2 mm beyond the tray outline
On the tray outline
5 mm short of the tray outline
mcqs.explain: So the sequence is denture extension, then tray outline 2 mm inside it, then spacer outline 2 mm inside that.

mcqs.q: Tissue stops are marked in which regions?
opts: Canine (2) and molar (2)
Incisor (2) and canine (2)
Premolar (2) only
The midline only
mcqs.explain: Four tissue stops in total: two canine and two molar.

mcqs.q: The spacer in the posterior palatal seal area should be:
opts: Bow shaped
Straight across the arch
V shaped
Absent from the palate entirely
mcqs.explain: This leaves the tray in direct contact with the tissue there so the posterior seal is recorded with slight displacement.

mcqs.q: The functions of the spacer are:
opts: To provide room for the impression material and to minimize pressure that could distort the mucosa
To orient the tray and give uniform material thickness
To prevent the acrylic sticking to the cast
To block out undercuts
mcqs.explain: Orienting the tray and ensuring uniform thickness are the functions of the tissue stops.

mcqs.q: The functions of the tissue stops are:
opts: To orient the tray and to give a uniform thickness of impression material
To provide room for the impression material
To develop the posterior palatal seal
To support the lip during the impression
mcqs.explain: They are windows cut in the wax spacer so the tray contacts the cast directly at those four points.

mcqs.q: Undercuts are blocked out with modelling wax in order to:
opts: Avoid breakage of the cast or the tray
Reduce the amount of impression material needed
Improve the border seal
Speed up the setting of the resin
mcqs.explain: Set acrylic that locks into an undercut fractures the cast, the tray, or both on removal.

mcqs.q: An undercut is defined as:
opts: A ridge or arch contour that prevents the insertion of a dental prosthesis
A contour that improves the retention of a dental prosthesis
The land area extending beyond the replica surface of a cast
The wax strip attached around the border of an impression
mcqs.explain: The last option describes the land area.

mcqs.q: The separating medium used before applying tray acrylic works by forming:
opts: Insoluble calcium alginate, from sodium alginate plus calcium sulfate
A soluble calcium chloride film
A layer of petroleum jelly
Calcium sulfate dihydrate
mcqs.explain: It is applied so that the acrylic resin does not stick to the cast.

mcqs.q: The accepted polymer-to-monomer ratio for tray resin is:
opts: 3 : 1 by volume
1 : 3 by volume
1 : 1 by volume
2 : 1 by weight
mcqs.explain: Properly proportioned, the mix produces a workable mass that passes through five stages on standing.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the five stages of the acrylic mix?
opts: Sandy, stringy, dough, rubbery, stiff
Stringy, sandy, dough, stiff, rubbery
Dough, sandy, stringy, rubbery, stiff
Sandy, dough, stringy, stiff, rubbery
mcqs.explain: The rubbery stage is also described as elastic.

mcqs.q: The tray material is adapted to the cast during which stage?
opts: The dough stage
The sandy stage
The stringy stage
The rubbery stage
mcqs.explain: Earlier the mix is sticky and uncontrollable; later it will no longer flow.

mcqs.q: The functions of the tray handle are:
opts: To support the lip during the impression and to help load, place and orient the tray
To stabilize the tray and distribute pressure equally
To provide room for the impression material
To orient the tray on the tissue stops
mcqs.explain: Stabilizing the tray and distributing pressure are the functions of the finger rests.

mcqs.q: The stated dimensions of the tray handle are:
opts: 3–4 mm thick, 8–10 mm long, 8–10 mm wide
8–10 mm thick, 3–4 mm long, 3–4 mm wide
2–3 mm thick, 15–17 mm long, 8–10 mm wide
1–2 mm thick, 5 mm long, 5 mm wide
mcqs.explain: It must support the lip rather than displace it.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a function of finger rests?
opts: Supporting the lip while making the impression
Stabilizing the tray in the mouth
Equal distribution of pressure
Reducing pressure applied to the tissues
mcqs.explain: Supporting the lip is a function of the handle.

mcqs.q: The recommended thickness of the tray periphery and of the rest of the tray is:
opts: Periphery 2–3 mm with rounded edges; the rest about 2 mm
Periphery 5 mm; the rest about 3 mm
Periphery 2 mm; the rest 5 mm
Uniform 1 mm throughout
mcqs.explain: Sharp tray edges injure the sulcus and ruin the border molding.

mcqs.q: Border molding is defined as the shaping of the border areas of an impression material by:
opts: Functional or manual manipulation of the soft tissue adjacent to the borders
Trimming the borders with an acrylic bur
Adding wax to the periphery on the cast
Vibrating the tray against the tissues
mcqs.explain: The aim is to duplicate the contour and size of the vestibule.

mcqs.q: The materials used for border molding are:
opts: Low-fusing compound and putty consistency of elastomeric impression materials
Zinc oxide eugenol paste and irreversible hydrocolloid
Baseplate wax and modelling wax
Dental stone and plaster
mcqs.explain: Low-fusing compound is supplied as green sticks softened in a flame; putty is mixed and moulded in one step.

mcqs.q: The wax spacer is removed:
opts: After border molding, without dislodging the border molding
Before border molding begins
After the final impression has been taken
Only if the tray is too tight
mcqs.explain: The spacer keeps the tray at the correct height on the tissue stops while the borders are being molded.

mcqs.q: The final impression is also correctly called the:
opts: Master impression
Preliminary impression
Secondary impression, which is the preferred term
Primary impression
mcqs.explain: The term secondary impression is described as not a good term.

mcqs.q: Materials used for the final impression in a custom tray are:
opts: Zinc oxide eugenol paste and medium- and light-body elastomeric materials
Impression compound and impression plaster
Putty elastomers and alginate
Dental stone and beading wax
mcqs.explain: Only medium and light bodies are used because the tray is already accurate and only a thin wash is required.

mcqs.q: A definitive cast is defined as:
opts: A replica of the residual ridge and dental arch used to fabricate a prosthesis
An interim base supporting the rim material for jaw records
An individualized tray made for taking a final impression
A strip of wax attached around the border of an impression
mcqs.explain: It is also called the final cast or master cast; a reproduction of a prepared tooth is a die.

mcqs.q: Master casts are made from:
opts: Alpha hemihydrate — dental stone
Beta hemihydrate — model plaster
Impression plaster
Calcium sulfate anhydrite
mcqs.explain: Alpha hemihydrate is denser and stronger than the beta form used for plaster.

mcqs.q: Which pouring method is used for MASTER casts?
opts: Beading and boxing method
Inversion method
Double-pour method
Free-flow method
mcqs.explain: The inversion method is used for preliminary casts; it would destroy the border detail of a master impression.

mcqs.q: The land area is defined as:
opts: The portion of a dental cast that extends beyond the impression's replica surface laterally
The deepest part of the palatal vault on the cast
The base of the cast below the ridge
The area of the cast covered by the wax spacer
mcqs.explain: It is the flat shelf created by the beading wax, which protects the delicate border roll.

mcqs.q: Boxing an impression is defined as:
opts: Enclosing an impression to form the base of the cast and preserve detail
Attaching a wax strip around the border of an impression
Trimming the land area of a cast to 2 to 3 mm
Indexing a cast so it can be remounted accurately
mcqs.explain: Attaching the strip below the border is beading, which precedes boxing.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an advantage of beading and boxing?
opts: It shortens the setting time of the stone
Superior hardness of the cast surface
It provides a land area
It preserves the borders of the impression
mcqs.explain: The fourth advantage is that it minimizes trimming.

mcqs.q: Master casts are poured with dental stone in a proportion of:
opts: 100 g of stone to 28–30 ml of water
100 g of stone to 45–50 ml of water
100 g of stone to 19–24 ml of water
100 g of stone to 60 ml of water
mcqs.explain: This is the standard stone water/powder ratio of 0.28–0.30; the cast is then left to set for about an hour.

mcqs.q: After beading and boxing, the poured cast is allowed to set for:
opts: About an hour
About five minutes
About 24 hours
Only until the surface gloss is lost
mcqs.explain: The tray is then placed in hot water before separation.

mcqs.q: Before separating the cast from the impression, the tray with the cast is placed in hot water in order to:
opts: Soften the low-fusing compound
Accelerate the setting of the stone
Dissolve the separating medium
Harden the surface of the cast
mcqs.explain: The compound is rigid at mouth temperature and locked into the land area; softening it prevents the cast borders from breaking off.

mcqs.q: The dimensions given for a completed master cast are:
opts: Land 2–3 mm, base 15–17 mm thick, vestibular depth 2–3 mm
Land 15–17 mm, base 2–3 mm thick, vestibular depth 2–3 mm
Land 5 mm, base 10 mm thick, vestibular depth 5 mm
Land 2–3 mm, base 5–7 mm thick, vestibular depth 10 mm
mcqs.explain: A cast with an insufficient base eventually fractures, necessitating remaking of the impression.

mcqs.q: Indexing the master cast is done in order to:
opts: Accurately remount the cast on an articulator
Identify the patient's name on the cast
Reduce the weight of the base
Mark the position of the posterior palatal seal
mcqs.explain: The index grooves fit the mounting stone in only one position, which is what makes laboratory remounting of the finished denture possible.

saqs.q: Define a custom tray and list the reasons for using one.
saqs.a: A CUSTOM TRAY is an individualized impression tray made from a cast recovered from a preliminary impression, used in making a FINAL impression. REASONS — to confine and control the final impression material; to obtain minute details of the denture-bearing area; to develop the border seal; to ensure uniform distribution of the impression material; and to ensure planned distribution of pressure on the residual ridges.

ans.text: An individualized impression tray made from a cast recovered from a preliminary impression, used in making the final impression.

list: To confine and control the final impression material
To obtain minute details of the denture-bearing area
To ensure uniform distribution of the final impression material
To ensure planned distribution of pressure on the residual ridges

saqs.q: Compare chemically-cured and visible light-cured custom tray materials.
saqs.a: CHEMICALLY-CURED (CC) acrylic resin — rigid, easy to fabricate, easy to trim and adjust, and inexpensive; disadvantages are polymerization shrinkage, the need for a time interval between fabrication and use, and the hazards of the monomer (methyl methacrylate), including dermatologic reactions. VISIBLE LIGHT-CURED (VLC) — chemically urethane dimethacrylate, supplied in sheet and gel forms, the SHEET form used for trays; advantages are that it is less hazardous, reduces preparation time, is easy to use and handles well; disadvantages are that it is brittle, produces fine particles on grinding, and needs a special curing chamber.

saqs.q: Describe how the cast is marked out before a custom tray is built, and explain why a spacer and tissue stops are used.
saqs.a: FIRST, mark the anticipated final extension of the denture in pencil on the cast. SECOND, mark the tray extension about 2 mm SHORTER than that line, except in the posterior palatal seal area. THIRD, mark the spacer outline 2 mm short of the tray outline, and mark the tissue stops in the canine (2) and molar (2) regions; the spacer in the posterior palatal seal should be BOW SHAPED. The SPACER provides room for the impression material and minimizes pressure that could distort the mucosa. The TISSUE STOPS orient the tray and give a uniform thickness of impression material.

steps: Mark the anticipated final extension of the denture in pencil on the cast
Mark the tray extension about 2 mm shorter than that line — except in the posterior palatal seal area
Mark the spacer outline 2 mm short of the tray outline, and the tissue stops in the canine (2) and molar (2) regions. The spacer in the posterior palatal seal should be bow shaped

saqs.q: Describe the mixing and adaptation of chemically-cured tray resin.
saqs.a: The accepted POLYMER-to-MONOMER ratio is 3 : 1 BY VOLUME. Mixed in the proper proportions the mass passes through five stages — sandy, stringy, DOUGH, rubbery/elastic, and stiff — and it is adapted to the cast over the wax spacer in the DOUGH stage. A HANDLE 3–4 mm thick, 8–10 mm long and 8–10 mm wide is added to support the lip during the impression and to help load, place and orient the tray. FINGER RESTS are added to hold the tray in position, stabilize it, give equal distribution of pressure and reduce pressure on the tissues. The cured tray periphery should be 2–3 mm thick with rounded edges and the rest of the tray about 2 mm thick.

ans.text: The accepted polymer : monomer ratio is 3 : 1 by volume.

saqs.q: Define border molding, list the materials used, and state what is done to the wax spacer afterwards.
saqs.a: BORDER MOLDING is the shaping of the border areas of an impression material by functional or manual manipulation of the adjacent soft tissue, to duplicate the contour and size of the vestibule. MATERIALS — low-fusing compound and the PUTTY consistency of elastomeric impression materials. AFTERWARDS the wax spacer is removed, taking care not to dislodge the border molding. The final (master) impression is then taken with zinc oxide eugenol paste or elastomers in medium and light body.

ans.text: The shaping of the border areas of an impression material by functional or manual manipulation of the adjacent soft tissue, to duplicate the contour and size of the vestibule.
Afterwards the wax spacer is removed, taking care not to dislodge the border molding. The final (master) impression is then taken with zinc oxide eugenol paste or elastomers in medium and light body.

saqs.q: Describe how a master cast is produced from the final impression, including beading, boxing, pouring, retrieval and the finished dimensions.
saqs.a: The DEFINITIVE (final/master) CAST is a replica of the residual ridge areas and/or other parts of the dental arch used to fabricate a prosthesis, made from ALPHA hemihydrate (dental stone). Casts are poured two ways — the INVERSION method for preliminary casts, and BEADING AND BOXING for master casts. BEADING attaches a strip of beading wax around the impression; BOXING encloses the impression to produce the desired size and form of the base and to preserve detail; the LAND is the part of the cast extending laterally beyond the replica surface. ADVANTAGES of beading and boxing — superior hardness of the cast surface, provision of a land area, preservation of the impression borders, and minimized trimming. The cast is poured with 100 g stone to 28–30 ml water and set about an hour; the tray and cast are then placed in HOT WATER to soften the low-fusing compound before careful separation. FINISHED DIMENSIONS — land 2–3 mm, base 15–17 mm thick, vestibule depth 2–3 mm; an insufficient base eventually fractures and the impression must be remade. Finally the cast is INDEXED, to remount it accurately on an articulator.

ans.text: The definitive cast — also the final or master cast — is a replica of the residual ridge areas and/or other parts of the dental arch used to fabricate a prosthesis, made from α-hemihydrate (dental stone).
